mn_picnic_rock.blurb: A compact cluster of boulders tucked at the foot of Sawmill Creek Dome in northeastern Minnesota, widely regarded as the best bouldering in the state. The stone is anorthosite, which looks and feels like granite, with enough texture that a long session leaves the fingertips sore. Problems run from the easiest grades up to the double digits, so there is something for most levels, and the setting is quiet and wooded rather than roadside. You reach it on foot along a forest trail, so bring pads and water for the hike. The season is short: spring can be good, but late September and October are usually the best, sometimes stretching into November.
mn_picnic_rock.approach: Walk the Superior Hiking Trail from the trailhead for roughly two miles to the signed spur marked for Picnic Rock, then follow the spur along the foot of the dome for a few minutes to the main boulders.

mn_eldon.blurb: Quiet sandstone bouldering on a wooded parcel beside the Kettle River near the town of Sandstone, now part of Banning State Park. The boulders are a fine-grained, coffee-colored sandstone with weathered ripples and curled edges for holds; some blocks are big enough to resemble small cottages and stand free among the trees. The problem count is modest, but they span a wide range from easy to very hard, and the area suits climbers who like movement over height. The stone is porous and weakens when wet, so give it at least two dry sunny days after rain. Late summer and fall are the most pleasant, once bugs and poison ivy ease off; high water on the river can flood part of the site.

mn_silver_creek_tunnel_rock.blurb: A roadside cliff on the North Shore of Lake Superior, next to the highway tunnel about eight miles north of Two Harbors. Most of the climbing is bolted sport routes, with a handful of trad lines mixed in, and the grades center on 5.9 to 5.11 with a few easier and harder outliers. The cliff is fairly tall and sits well above the lake, though most routes are shorter than a full rope length. Some of the stone has been cleaned while other patches remain loose, so wear a helmet. The same cliff is also a popular winter ice climbing spot. A paved path runs right beneath the wall and is shared with walkers and bikers.
mn_silver_creek_tunnel_rock.parking_note: Leave the car at the scenic pull-off by the southern tunnel on the old highway alignment, then walk up the paved trail to the base of the cliff.
mn_silver_creek_tunnel_rock.approach: Short walk up the paved bike path from the pull-off to the foot of the cliff.

mt_pine_creek.blurb: Pine Creek is a drainage on the east side of Paradise Valley, south of Livingston, and it holds two very different kinds of climbing. Up high is a scattering of boulders in a gully and talus field below Pine Creek Lake, on quartz blocks and mica fins, with many problems starting in pits or caves that are hard to find without photos. It feels remote and alpine, reached by hiking the trail toward the lakes, and snow lingers late at that elevation. In winter a few short ice flows form in the canyon, rated roughly WI2 to WI3+. Most of the climbing here is on the boulders, from easy to hard.

mt_main_crag.blurb: The busiest wall at Allenspur, a sport climbing area on limestone and dolomite above the Yellowstone River in Paradise Valley south of Livingston. All of the climbing is bolted, with most lines falling between 5.10 and 5.12 and a few easier ones at the low end, and routes usually take around ten draws. It gets morning shade and afternoon sun, so summer afternoons can run hot, while spring and fall are the comfortable seasons. Watch for loose rock. The trail crosses private land, so stay on the path.
mt_main_crag.parking_note: Use the Carter Bridge fishing access off East River Road; do not leave cars along the road where the climbers' trail turns uphill.
mt_main_crag.approach: From the fishing access walk down East River Road for a short distance, then take the climbers' trail east up to Boundary Crag and continue left (north) a few minutes along the base to reach Main Crag.

nv_hercules_gap.blurb: A limestone slot canyon near Ely in eastern Nevada, cut by a lightly traveled paved road, with walls on both sides of it. Nearly all of the climbing is bolted sport, plus a few trad lines and some boulder problems. Grades start easy but most routes fall in the 5.10 to 5.13 range, and the pumpy limestone suits climbers who like to work harder lines. The biggest concentration of routes is in the Cave Sector, roughly halfway through the canyon on the left when entering from the east. It sits at around 6,300 feet, so expect cooler temperatures than the valley floor.
nv_hercules_gap.parking_note: Pull off at either end of the canyon road, which runs through the gap; enter from the east side to find the Cave Sector.

nv_the_wake_up_wall.blurb: A short, dense sandstone cliff in the Sandstone Quarry area of Red Rock Canyon, near Las Vegas. Routes are mostly bolted and punchy, with a few trad lines, ranging from about 5.8 into the 5.12s with the bulk at 5.10 to 5.12. It faces northeast and stays shaded for most of a winter day, so it works well as a warm-up or on warmer days. The sandstone is fragile when wet and can be permanently damaged, so stay off it during and after rain and while the ground is damp. Belays are in a pit at the base, and a flat slab nearby makes a handy staging spot.
nv_the_wake_up_wall.parking_note: Park in the Sandstone Quarry lot off the Red Rock loop road and start up the signed trail from there.
nv_the_wake_up_wall.approach: From the lot take the Calico Tanks trail to the fork, go left on the signed Turtlehead Peak trail, and after a short steep rise head straight or left over slabs to the base. About 0.4 miles.
